concepts.decision: Match methods to the claim and report scope, assumptions, coverage, limitations, findings, owner, and retest plan.
concepts.definition: A structured evaluation of whether software security requirements, controls, evidence, and residual risks are adequate for the stated claim.
concepts.failureExample: A checklist that never tests the privileged export path cannot establish that authorization is effective.
concepts.label: Software Assessment

concepts.decision: Select methods from threat and lifecycle stage; use realistic roles/data and state what paths or configurations were not covered.
concepts.definition: Testing of application security behavior through appropriate methods such as review, SAST, DAST, IAST, dependency checks, fuzzing, abuse cases, interface tests, and configuration tests.
concepts.failureExample: An unauthenticated scan cannot prove privileged-role access control is enforced.
concepts.label: Appsec Testing

concepts.decision: Choose metrics tied to a decision and pair volume/speed with severity, exposure, exceptions, outcome evidence, and potential gaming.
concepts.definition: Quantitative measures used to understand security control performance, trends, coverage, exposure, timeliness, or outcomes.
concepts.failureExample: A high closure percentage can hide indefinitely accepted internet-facing critical vulnerabilities.
concepts.label: Security Metrics

concepts.decision: Monitor signals that relate to stated threats and response decisions; tune ownership, escalation, coverage, and feedback into engineering.
concepts.definition: Ongoing observation of deployed software behavior, configuration, performance, security events, and anomalies.
concepts.failureExample: A control may pass pre-release tests but fail in production due to a changed identity or configuration.
concepts.label: Runtime Monitoring

concepts.decision: Prioritize with exploitability, exposure, impact, dependencies, compensating controls, and owner; retest remediation and review exceptions.
concepts.definition: The lifecycle of identifying, validating, prioritizing, assigning, remediating or accepting, verifying, and tracking vulnerability risk.
concepts.failureExample: Closing a ticket after applying a patch without verifying the running version leaves exposure unknown.
concepts.label: Vulnerability Management

concepts.decision: Log sufficient actor/action/target/time/outcome/correlation context without secrets; protect integrity and verify alerts/queries lead to action.
concepts.definition: Generation, protection, retention, and analysis of security-relevant records that support detection, investigation, accountability, and response.
concepts.failureExample: Verbose logs that include tokens create a new disclosure risk while still failing to identify who authorized an export.
concepts.label: Logging

misconceptions.claim: A passed scan proves an application is secure.
misconceptions.correction: Scans have coverage and false-negative limits; use layered evidence and operational feedback.

outcome: Build an evidence plan that evaluates whether software controls reduce risk through development and operation.

sections.body: Assess requirements traceability, threat-model coverage, design and code review, SAST/DAST/IAST where suitable, dependency and container checks, abuse-case and interface tests, deployment configuration, logs, vulnerability age, incident outcomes, and remediation retests. Match each method to a claim and state coverage and limitations.
keyPoints: Testing evidence should connect to requirements and threats.
Runtime evidence validates assumptions made before deployment.
Metrics need context, trends, and defined response thresholds.
sections.title: Use layered evidence

sections.body: Combine findings with exploitability, business impact, exposure, exceptions, and control operation. Feed results into backlog, change, patch, incident, and architecture decisions. Logging should support detection and investigation without leaking secrets; effectiveness includes response speed and learning, not only defect counts.
keyPoints: A low defect count can reflect weak testing or telemetry.
Risk-based prioritization prevents tool volume from driving every decision.
sections.title: Measure and improve

sections.body: Audit and logging of changes should connect an authorized request, identity, code/configuration revision, reviewer, test evidence, deployment target, time, and rollback or emergency path. Assess effectiveness by comparing the control claim and threat to observed prevention, detection, response, and recovery evidence. Analyze likelihood, impact, exploitability, exposure, dependencies, and compensating controls; select mitigation, transfer, avoidance, acceptance, or redesign with an accountable owner and retest plan.
keyPoints: A log is evidence only when complete, protected, time-correlated, and reviewed for the stated claim.
Risk analysis explains why a finding matters and which mitigation changes residual risk.
Trend and outcome evidence are stronger than raw scan or backlog counts.
sections.title: Audit changes and connect evidence to risk reduction

learningJob.plainExplanation: A passed scan is one evidence stream rather than proof that an application is secure. Judge effectiveness against defined threats and flows using layered tests, runtime evidence, remediation, and retest.
learningJob.visualReasoningGain: An evidence map could compare claim, threat, test coverage, observed failures, runtime outcomes, remediation, and retest; the opening claim/SAST/test boxes do not decompose sufficiency.
